title: OpenAI Claims to Prove the Ultimate Limit of Matrix Multiplication: The Optimal Algorithm Exponent Is Exactly 9/4

content_html:
Last month it proved half; this month it pieced together the other half. On November 24, OpenAI released a preprint claiming to have proved that the matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4—in October it first proved ω ≤ 9/4, and now it has proved ω ≥ 9/4. The upper and lower bounds close, yielding an equality.

ω Characterizes the Theoretical Optimum

The matrix multiplication exponent ω describes the asymptotic power exponent governing how, when n is sufficiently large, the number of arithmetic operations required by the optimal algorithm for multiplying two n×n matrices grows with n; more rigorously, ω is the infimum of all attainable complexity exponents. This quantity matters because matrix multiplication is widely used, and fields such as machine learning and image processing all depend on it; ω not only characterizes the optimal exponent of theoretical algorithms in the asymptotic sense, but is also related to a series of important complexity problems.

If the Proof Holds, 9/4 Is a Line You Can Go Above but Not Below

If OpenAI's proof is correct, the conclusion is bidirectional: for any X > 9/4, there exists a matrix multiplication algorithm and a constant CX > 0 such that for all sufficiently large n, its number of arithmetic operations is no more than CX·nX; for any Y < 9/4, there is no algorithm together with a constant CY > 0 that can push the number of operations down to within CY·nY.

At the same time, it leaves room for caveats: ω is an asymptotic quantity, corresponding to the result as matrix size tends to infinity; practical applications are also affected by constant factors, memory access, parallel computing, hardware architecture, and other factors. The preprint has been posted to OpenAI's GitHub math repository.
